name: Pre-colonial Philippine states
summary: Barangay communities and small kingdoms of the Philippine islands, such as Tondo, Maynila and Cebu, that traded with China and Borneo before Spain conquered most of the islands from 1565.

terrain.value: Over 7,000 islands with narrow coastal plains, river valleys such as the Pasig, and mountain ranges like the Cordillera of northern Luzon.

climate.value: Tropical and humid, with a wet monsoon from about June to October and frequent typhoons, especially in Luzon and the Visayas.

resources.value: Rice, coconuts, gold from Butuan and Paracale, forest goods such as beeswax and hardwoods, pearls and sea products.

disasters.value: Typhoons, floods and earthquakes, and eruptions of active volcanoes such as Taal and Mayon.

population.value: The page gives no total. Barangays had 20 to 100 families on the coast, and population density is thought to have been low.
population.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1565) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages and farming land around a royal capital.

disease.value: Tropical diseases such as malaria; Spanish contact after 1521 brought new epidemics, but early records are few.

migration.value: Chinese and Malay traders settled in ports; Muslim traders and teachers from Borneo and the Malay world came to Sulu, Mindanao and Manila.

economicBase.value: Trade with China began in the Tang dynasty and grew under the Song. A debt in the Laguna Copperplate was worth 926.4 grams of gold. Rice farming is not mentioned.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1565) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

tradeRoutes.value: The earliest suggested direct Chinese contact is 982, when Ma-i merchants reached Guangzhou and Quanzhou.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1521) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

wealth.value: Gold was plentiful: finds such as the Surigao treasure show fine jewellery, and Chinese porcelain was buried with the dead.

moneyAndTax.value: Small gold pieces called piloncitos, gold by weight, and barter; datus received rice and labour from their followers.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; some slavery or bonded labour.

governmentType.value: City-states formed from barangays, each led by a datu and made up of about a hundred families.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1521) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

keyRulers.value: Lapulapu was chief of Mactan, an enemy of Datu Zula of Cebu. Rajah Sulayman and Rajah Humabon are not described on the page.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1565) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Datu rank usually passed to a son, but a datu also needed wealth, courage and followers to keep power.

institutions.value: Customary law applied by datus and elders, with disputes settled by fines or ordeals; there was no single central state.

stability.value: Many small barangays and rajahnates competed; alliances by marriage and raids for captives were common.

eliteConflict.value: Rival datus fought over followers and trade; Rajah Humabon of Cebu and Lapulapu of Mactan were rivals in 1521.

armyAndTech.value: Warriors used the kampilan sword, spears and shields, sailed karakoa warships, and by the 1500s had some lantaka bronze cannons.

majorWars.value: At the Battle of Mactan on 27 April 1521, Magellan and 14 of his men were killed by Lapulapu's forces. Manila's 1570–71 resistance is not mentioned (the page dates Maynila to about 1500–1571).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1565) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Spain took Cebu (1565) and Manila (1571), then most of Luzon and the Visayas; Muslim Sulu and Maguindanao stayed independent.

alliancesRivals.value: Close links with Brunei, whose royal family was tied to Maynila’s rulers; tribute missions to Ming China; rivalry with Sulu and among datus.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled boat-building and fine goldwork stand out.

scienceEducation.value: Baybayin script was widely used for short texts; the Laguna Copperplate Inscription (900) shows earlier writing in the Kawi script.

openness.value: Very open to trade: Chinese junks visited ports such as Tondo, Maynila and Cebu, and Islam spread along trade links.

communicationTransport.value: Balangay and other plank boats along coasts and between islands, rivers such as the Pasig, and footpaths inland.

religion.value: The article credits Makhdum Karim with bringing Islam to the archipelago in 1380.
religion.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1521) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

languageWriting.value: Tagalog, Visayan and others; Baybayin script.

artsArchitecture.value: Gold jewellery and burial masks, carved wood, and houses of wood and bamboo raised on stilts.

sharedIdentity.value: People identified with their barangay, datu and kin group rather than with the islands as a whole.

dailyLife.value: Village families grew rice and root crops, fished, chewed betel nut and lived in raised houses near rivers and coasts.

neighbours.value: The Sultanate of Brunei, the Sulu Sultanate, Ming China, the Malay ports and, from 1521, Spanish and Portuguese ships.

ideasReligions.value: Islam spread from Borneo and Sulu: the Sulu Sultanate formed in the 1400s, and Muslim rajahs ruled Maynila by the 1500s.

riseSignals.value: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription is dated to 900 (822 in the Saka calendar).
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1521) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: The page does not describe a peak. Butuan is dated before 989 to 1521 and Maynila about 1500–1571; trade with Brunei is not described.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1565) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: Spanish arrival: Magellan in 1521 and Legazpi from 1565, followed by the conquest of Cebu, Panay and Manila.

outcome.value: Magellan’s expedition reached Homonhon on 16 March 1521.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: History of the Philippines (900–1521) (checked 13 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and foreign reports; figures are estimates.
